entries.content:
There is, within me, a persistent sense of division—a consciousness that is not singular, but rather composed of two contending natures. I have often reflected, with a grave and almost mournful clarity, on the fact that my life has been shaped by this profound duplicity. One side aspires to uprightness, to the relief of sorrow and the advancement of knowledge; the other, more primitive, is drawn to pleasures I have concealed, irregularities I have hidden with a sense of shame. These are not mere passing moods, but distinct provinces of my soul, each with its own memories, desires, and even a sense of self. Though I have not always named them, I have come to recognize their roles: one, the just and aspiring, and the other, the unjust, freed from remorse. My scientific inquiries have only deepened this awareness, revealing that man is not truly one, but truly two—bound together in a trembling, agonized consciousness, each struggling for supremacy.

entries.content:
Authority and obedience—those are the levers that pry open the cracks in my soul. When the weight of command or the expectation of submission presses down, it is not the upright, aspiring side that rises, but the other—the one that writhes beneath the surface, hungry for release. In the presence of power, I have felt the urge to defy, to cast off the trembling garment of restraint and let the unjust, primitive self take the reins. Obedience, too, can be a mask, a way to conceal the true nature that seethes within. The more exacting the demand, the more I feel the provinces of good and ill within me sever, the more I long to be freed from the aspirations and remorse of my so-called better half. It is a curse, this binding together of polar twins, and in moments of authority—whether wielded or endured—the struggle for supremacy becomes a violent, almost ecstatic agony. I have learned to hide, to wear a grave countenance, but beneath it, the lower elements of my soul wait, eager for any chance to dethrone the upright and seize control.

entries.content:
Yes, I have, on occasion, surrendered control—deliberately, almost as an experiment—to that side of myself which is guided by uprightness and moral aspiration. In those moments, I endeavored to advance knowledge, to relieve sorrow, and to conduct myself with the utmost integrity before others. The impact on my relationships was, at least outwardly, positive: I was regarded with respect, even trust. Yet, beneath this surface, I could not escape the sense of duplicity, for the other side—the primitive, unjust nature—remained ever present, concealed but not extinguished. This surrender to morality brought with it a certain peace, but also a persistent anxiety, for I knew that my virtue was, in part, a performance, and that the struggle within me was unresolved. My perception of my own morality became more complex: I was not a hypocrite, for I truly strove to do good, but I was also painfully aware that this was only one half of my nature, and that the other, if left unchecked, might one day assert itself with terrible force.
